name: Chaima
confidence_why: Álvarez 2018, the only modern description, states that the colonial sources do not allow the stressed syllable to be determined and presents his penult-or-final pattern as a reading convention adopted by analogy with Kari'ña, Biord Castillo 2018 likewise calls the suprasegmentals only partially documented, and the one colonial grammar of Chaima, Tauste 1680, says nothing about accent (confirmed by Sánchez Méndez 2012), so the sources agree that no stress rule is recoverable, but they are few.
catalog_citation: Álvarez, José. 2018. Kure mana choto maimuru (Nuestra lengua está viva). Bosquejo gramatical, fraseología, léxico básico y textos de la extinta lengua caribana de la costa nororiental de Venezuela, hablada antiguamente por cumanagotos, chaimas, palenques, guaiqueríes, pariagotos, cuacas, píritus, cores, teques, mariches, y otros. Maracaibo: Universidad del Zulia (edición electrónica). recovered from the Internet Archive capture (2022-04-12) of the academia.edu page.
catalog_locator: p. 11, section 'La sílaba tónica' (page numbers head each page and match the Índice at: 'La sílaba tónica 11'); p. 12 'La elisión de vocales finales'.
catalog_quote: Las fuentes con las que contamos para el conocimiento de la lengua caribana no nos permiten saber con exactitud cómo se determinaba la sílaba tónica de la palabra. Sin embargo, pensamos que se parecía más al kari’ña, más próximo geográficamente al caribano, que al pemón. En pemón, todas las palabras, con algunas excepciones, son agudas. En kari’ña, el acento principal recae en la última o antepenúltima sílaba. Para la lectura de las palabras en caribano, hemos adoptado aquí el siguiente principio: La sílaba tónica, la que recibe el acento, es la penúltima si la palabra termina en sílaba abierta: kamare ke ‘lejos’, penare ‘hace mucho tiempo’, tawarune ‘oscuro’, ... Pero si la última es trabada/cerrada (termina en consonante), o si contiene un diptongo, dicha sílaba es la tónica: tupon ken ‘criollo’, te mukasen ‘castrado’, ... kospai ‘anoche’, petoi ‘compañero’, asorowau ‘tres’, ... En los ejemplos anteriores hemos destacado en negritas la sílaba tónica. Por otra parte, aunque sospechamos la existencia del fenómeno métrico conocido como alargamiento yámbico, presente en pemón y kari’ña, las fuentes caribanas no nos permiten establecer inequívocamente este fenómeno.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: The sources we have for the Caribana language do not allow us to know exactly how the tonic syllable of the word was determined. However, we think it resembled Kari'ña, geographically closer to Caribano, more than Pemón. [...] For reading Caribano words we have adopted here the following principle: the tonic syllable, the one that receives the accent, is the penult if the word ends in an open syllable: kamareke 'far', penare [...] But if the last syllable is checked/closed (ends in a consonant), or if it contains a diphthong, that syllable is the tonic: tuponken 'criollo', [...] kospai 'last night', petoi 'companion'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress placement in Chaima/Cumanagoto ('lengua caribana') is NOT recoverable from the colonial documentation; the only modern description says so explicitly and then prescribes an orthoepic convention for revitalization use (penult when the final syllable is open, final when it is closed or contains a diphthong), chosen by analogy with Kari'ña. The convention is the author's, not an attested fact about the language.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing; author adds that iambic lengthening (as in Pemón and Kari'ña) is suspected but cannot be established from the sources (p.12).
new_statements.exceptions: p.12-13: when a word-final vowel is elided the tonic syllable stays the same (open penult becomes closed final): yesemo > yesen, apanarü > apanar — again within the adopted convention.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; statement covers the whole coastal language (Cumanagoto, Chaima, Guaiquerí etc. dialects) reconstructed from Tauste 1680 (Chaima), Yangues/Ruiz Blanco (Cumanagoto), Tapia, Caulín. The one primary Chaima grammar (Tauste 1680) is silent on accent (confirmed by Sánchez Méndez 2012:132); Humboldt 1816:311-312 only remarks that Chayma has 'moins de terminaisons sonores en voyelles accentuées' than Carib or Sáliva.
new_statements.identity_note: Álvarez 2018 describes the 'lengua caribana / choto maimuru', i.e. the single coastal Cariban language whose dialects include Cumanagoto (cuma1240), Chaima (chai1253), Guaiquerí, Palenque, Píritu etc. — Glottolog's 'Cumana' node coas1302. His statement on the tonic syllable therefore applies equally to chai1253 and cuma1240 and is based on the same colonial corpus (Tauste 1680 for Chaima; Yangues 1683/Ruiz Blanco 1690 for Cumanagoto). Note that Yangues 1683 (Cumanagoto, held under cuma1240) does give accent placement for a few specific verb forms, which Álvarez does not use; nothing comparable exists in Tauste for Chaima.
